analysis.one_liner: Sets minimum nurse-to-patient staffing ratios in hospitals and protects nurses who refuse unsafe assignments.
analysis.headline: The bill had 43 House supporters, all Democrats, but never received a committee or floor vote and died when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require every hospital in the country to meet minimum nurse-to-patient ratios — for example, one nurse per four patients on medical-surgical units and one per two in intensive care. It would ban averaging and mandatory overtime to meet the ratios, require hospitals to post their actual staffing, and let nurses refuse assignments that violate the ratios or that they are not trained for, with protection from retaliation. Hospitals would get Medicare payment adjustments to cover compliance costs, and the bill adds nursing scholarships and retention grants.
analysis.who_benefits: Hospital patients, who get more nursing care per patient and lower risk of medical errors, and registered nurses and licensed practical nurses, who get enforceable workloads, an end to mandatory-overtime staffing, and legal protection for refusing unsafe assignments.

how_it_helps.text: Hospitals must implement staffing plans meeting fixed minimum direct-care registered-nurse-to-patient ratios by unit, ranging from 1:1 in trauma and operating rooms to 1:6 in well-baby nurseries [S3].

Hospitals may not average patient counts across units or shifts to meet the ratios, may not impose mandatory overtime to meet them, and may only allow a direct-care nurse to relieve another nurse during breaks [S3].

A nurse may refuse an assignment that violates the ratios or that she is not prepared for without compromising patient safety, and the hospital may not fire, retaliate against, or report her to a state licensing board for doing so [S3].
Hospitals must post actual nurse-to-patient ratios in each unit for staff, patients, and the public, keep three years of staffing records, and submit staffing plans to HHS for public inspection [S3].

HHS would adjust Medicare payments to hospitals to cover the additional cost of compliance, and the bill adds stipends to nursing scholarships and expands nurse retention grants with preceptorship and mentorship programs [S3].

Patients, nurses, and others could file complaints through a toll-free hotline; HHS would investigate, impose civil penalties of up to $25,000 per knowing violation, and publish violators' names online [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals, which would have to hire substantially more nurses and pay for them, though Medicare payment adjustments would offset the share of costs attributable to Medicare patients; ultimately federal spending and hospital operating budgets bear the cost.

drawbacks.text: Hiring enough nurses to meet the ratios is expensive, and the Medicare adjustment only covers the incremental cost attributable to Medicare beneficiaries, leaving hospitals to absorb the rest [S3].

The nation already has a nurse shortage, and the bill's own findings acknowledge ratios depend on recruiting and retaining nurses; if the workforce cannot grow fast enough, hospitals could struggle to fill shifts even with the two-year (four-year for rural hospitals) phase-in [S3].

Critics of fixed ratios argue they are less flexible than acuity-based staffing — a hospital could meet the ratio while patients are sicker than usual — though the bill addresses this by requiring transparent acuity systems and staffing above the minimums where patient acuity demands it [S3].
Costs could strain rural and small hospitals, which is why the bill gives them an extra two years to comply and exempts declared emergencies from the ratios [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The patient-safety benefits are substantial and the bill pairs the mandate with Medicare reimbursement and workforce investments, but it would be costly for hospitals and hard to staff during a nurse shortage; the phase-in periods and emergency exemptions acknowledge that strain.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to two House committees and their health subcommittees, but no markup, hearing, or floor vote ever happened, and it died when the 114th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jan Schakowsky introduced the bill on March 25, 2015, and it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee [S1].
Within days it was referred to the Health subcommittees of both committees, on March 27 and April 7, 2015, and no further action was taken for the rest of the Congress [S5].
The bill attracted 42 cosponsors, all Democrats, and none of them were on committees that moved it [S4].
The House took no vote on the bill before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospitals that keep nurse staffing lean came out ahead: no committee ever acted on the bill, so no new ratios, overtime limits, or staffing disclosures were ever imposed. Hospital patients and nurses got nothing from it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Hospitals that keep nurse staffing lean

sides.party_line_note: All 42 cosponsors were Democrats and the bill died in committees controlled by the Republican majority without a hearing or vote; no Republican supported it.

industries.note: The bill would force hospitals to hire significantly more nurses per shift, ban mandatory-overtime staffing, and publish actual ratios — costs that many hospitals currently avoid by running lean staffing, which is exactly what the ratios target. Medicare adjustments would offset some, not all, of the cost.
Mandatory higher staffing and a ban on covering gaps with overtime would increase hospitals' demand for temporary and agency nurses to fill open shifts.
New stipends for nursing scholarships and expanded retention grants with preceptorship and mentorship funding would channel federal money into training and retaining nurses.
